content: This report provides an update to the 2000 recommendations by the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) regarding the use of influenza vaccines and antiviral agents. The 2001 recommendations include new or revised information on the cost-effectiveness of influenza vaccination, the supply of influenza vaccines, neuraminidase-inhibitor antiviral drugs, the 2001-2002 trivalent vaccine virus strains (A/Moscow/10/99 [H3N2]-like, A/New Caledonia/20/99 [H1N1]-like, and B/Sichuan/379/99-like strains), and the extension of the optimal vaccination period through November. Influenza epidemics typically occur during winter months and are responsible for an average of approximately 20,000 deaths annually in the United States. Influenza viruses can also cause pandemics, during which illness and death rates from influenza-related complications can increase dramatically worldwide. Influenza affects all age groups, with the highest infection rates among children, but the highest rates of severe illness and death occur among individuals aged over 65 years and those with medical conditions that increase their risk of complications. Vaccination is the primary method for preventing influenza and its severe complications. Vaccination is associated with reductions in influenza-related respiratory illness, physician visits, hospitalizations, and deaths among high-risk individuals, as well as reductions in otitis media among children and work absenteeism among adults. Despite substantial increases in vaccination levels, further improvements are needed, particularly among high-risk individuals under 65 years of age. The 2001 recommendations include five principal changes: 1. Information on the cost-effectiveness of influenza vaccination has been added. 2. Information on the influenza vaccine supply has been added. 3. Updates on neuraminidase-inhibitor antiviral drugs have been included. 4. The 2001-2002 trivalent vaccine virus strains are specified as A/Moscow/10/99 (H3N2)-like, A/New Caledonia/20/99 (H1N1)-like, and B/Sichuan/379/99-like strains. 5. The recommended optimal time period for vaccination is October through November. Influenza A and B viruses are the two types that cause epidemic human disease. Influenza A viruses are further categorized into subtypes based on two surface antigens: hemagglutinin (H) and neuraminidase (N). Influenza B viruses are not categorized into subtypes. Since 1977, influenza A (H1N1), influenza A (H3N2), and influenza B viruses have been in global circulation. Both influenza A and B viruses undergo antigenic drift, resulting from point mutations during viral replication. Influenza B viruses undergo antigenic drift less rapidly than influenza A viruses. Immunity to surface antigens, particularly hemagglutinin, reduces the likelihood of infection and disease severity. However, antibody to one influenza virus type or subtype provides limited or no protection against another type or subtype. Frequent development of antigenic variants through antigenic drift is the virologic basis for seasonal epidemics and the reason for incorporating new strains into each year’s influenza vaccine. Influenza viruses are primarily spread from person to person through coughing and sneezing. The incubation period is 1-4 days, with an average of 2 days. Individuals can be infectious starting the day before symptoms begin and for approximately 5 days after illness onset, with children being infectious for longer periods. Symptoms include fever, myalgia, headache, severe malaise, nonproductive cough, sore throat, and rhinitis. Influenza-related respiratory illness is difficult to distinguish from illnesses caused by other respiratory pathogens based on symptoms alone. Influenza illness typically resolves after several days, although cough and malaise can persist for more than 2 weeks. Complications, particularly among individuals with underlying conditions, can include secondary bacterial pneumonia, primary influenza viral pneumonia, or co-infections with other pathogens. Influenza infection has also been associated with encephalopathy, transverse myelitis, Reye syndrome, myositis, myocarditis, and pericarditis. The risks for complications, hospitalizations, and deaths from influenza are higher among individuals aged over 65 years, very young children, and those with certain underlying health conditions. Estimated rates of influenza-associated hospitalizations vary by age group and epidemic. Among children aged 0-4 years, hospitalization rates range from approximately 500 per 100,000 population for those with high-risk conditions to 100 per 100,000 for those without high-risk conditions. Hospitalization rates are highest among children aged 0-1 years and are comparable to rates among individuals aged over 65 years. During influenza epidemics from 1969-1970 through 1994-1995, the estimated number of influenza-associated hospitalizations in the United States ranged from approximately 16,000 to 220,000 per epidemic, with an average of 114,000 excess hospitalizations per year. The greatest numbers of hospitalizations occurred during epidemics caused by type A (H3N2) viruses. Influenza-related deaths can result from pneumonia, exacerbations of cardiopulmonary conditions, and other chronic diseases. During 19 of 23 influenza epidemics, estimated rates of influenza-associated deaths ranged from approximately 30 to over 150 deaths per 100,000 persons aged over 65 years. Older adults account for over 90% of deaths attributed to pneumonia and influenza. Vaccinating high-risk individuals before the influenza season each year is the most effective means of reducing the impact of influenza. Vaccination coverage can be increased by administering vaccines during hospitalizations or routine health-care visits before the influenza season, reducing the need for special visits to physicians’ offices or clinics. Vaccination of residents and staff in nursing homes and other chronic-care facilities can reduce the risk of outbreaks by inducing herd immunity. Vaccination of health-care workers and others in close contact with high-risk individuals can also reduce transmission of influenza and subsequent complications. The use of influenza-specific antiviral drugs for chemoprophylaxis or treatment is an important adjunct to vaccination. However, antiviral medications are not a substitute for vaccination. The trivalent inactivated influenza vaccine prepared for the 2001-2002 season includes A/Moscow/10/99 (H3N2)-like, A/New Caledonia/20/99 (H1N1)-like, and B/Sichuan/379/99-like antigens. These viruses are used because of their growth properties and representativeness of currently circulating A (H3N2) and B viruses. The effectiveness of influenza vaccine depends on the age and immunocompetence of the recipient and the similarity between vaccine and circulating viruses. Most vaccinated children and young adults develop high post-vaccination hemagglutination-inhibition antibody titers, which are protective against illness caused by strains similar to those in the vaccine. When vaccine and circulating viruses are antigenically similar, influenza vaccine prevents illness in approximately 70%-90% of healthy individuals aged under 65 years. Vaccination of healthy adults has also resulted in decreased work absenteeism and reduced use of health-care resources, including antibiotics, when vaccine and circulating viruses are well-matched. Among elderly individuals, the vaccine is effective in preventing secondary complications and reducing the risk of hospitalization and death, even though it may be less effective in preventing influenza illness. Influenza vaccination can reduce both health-care costs and productivity losses associated with influenza illness. Economic studies have found overall societal cost savings and substantial reductions in hospitalizations and deaths among individuals aged over 65 years. Increasing vaccination coverage among high-risk individuals aged under 65 years, including children, is a high priority for expanding vaccine use. Annual vaccination is recommended for health-care workers, but vaccination rates among this group remain low. Vaccination of health-care workers has been associated with reduced work absenteeism and fewer deaths among nursing home patients. Influenza vaccination is strongly recommended for individuals aged over 6 months who are at increased risk for complications due to age or underlying medical conditions. Vaccination is also recommended for health-care workers and others in close contact with high-risk individuals to reduce transmission. Vaccination can be administered to any individual aged over 6 months to reduce the chance of influenza infection.
